article_content: An investigation by the Air Accident Investigation Branch (AAIB) has revealed that a Boeing 737 operating for Monarch Airlines veered off the runway at Birmingham Airport in September 2012 because it was traveling at more than double the recommended speed. The aircraft, carrying 137 passengers returning from Nice, France, reached 23 miles per hour during taxiing â far exceeding the standard limit of 11 mph. According to the report, the pilot was trying to vacate the runway swiftly to allow another plane to pass, which led to loss of control. As the aircraft turned, it began to skid sideways, eventually leaving the paved surface and coming to rest on the adjacent grass. Although the plane suffered significant damage to its wheels and tires, and passengers were thrown from their seats, miraculously, no one was hurt. Passengers described the moment as terrifying, with some fearing for their lives as the plane lurched toward the fence. The same aircraft had previously caused disruption in Tenerife the year before when a door failed, stranding 150 people. In response to the Birmingham incident, Monarch Airlines immediately ended its agreement with the Lithuanian carrier Aurela Airlines, which operated the flight. One passenger recalled a similar juddering sound during both takeoff in Nice and landing in Birmingham, suggesting possible mechanical issues.

article_content: Early Monday morning, Los Angeles firefighters responded to two separate apartment fires within hours of each otherâone in a building under construction and another in a building undergoing renovation. The first blaze erupted just before 1:30 a.m. at 906 N. Fremont Ave., directly across from a fire station. LAFD Chief Ralph Terrazas said the seven-story wood-frame structure covered approximately 1.3 million square feet, with over two-thirds of the building fully engulfed in flames. The intensity of the fire posed serious risks to neighboring high-rise buildings. More than 250 firefighters worked tirelessly to bring the fire under control. Thankfully, no injuries were reported. Andrew Gottesman, a local resident and CNN iReporter, watched the fire from his window and described it as 'incredibly large' and 'nerve-racking,' saying he feared he might have to evacuate his own building. About eight blocks away, a second fire broke out around 4 a.m. on West Seventh Street in a smaller residential building. Though smaller in scale, it still required 100 firefighters to extinguish. Authorities have not linked the two incidents, and investigations into their causes are ongoing. Both fires led to temporary closures of the 110 and 101 freeways, causing major traffic delays. Estimated damages are still being assessed but are expected to reach the multimillion-dollar range.

article_content: In a massive poll of over 250,000 film enthusiasts, Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back has been crowned the greatest movie of all time. Released in 1980 â three years after the original Star Wars â the film edged out Francis Ford Coppolaâs The Godfather for the top spot, with The Dark Knight coming in third. The Shawshank Redemption and Pulp Fiction rounded out the top five. George Lucas, the creator of Star Wars, called it a 'privilege' to see his film top the list. He noted that fans often favor The Empire Strikes Back because of its darker tone â a defining trait of its position as the middle chapter in the original trilogy. 'I never planned for Star Wars to be three separate films,' Lucas said. 'But once it became that, each one developed its own personality through the story.' Other classics in the top 10 include the original Star Wars, Raiders of the Lost Ark, and Jaws. Mark Dinning, editor-in-chief of Empire magazine, said, 'Weâre delighted â if not surprised â that The Empire Strikes Back has been voted the greatest film of all time by hundreds of thousands of readers. It made Star Wars both epic and deeply personal when it premiered, and today, it still holds that same power, wit, heart, and spectacle.' With J.J. Abrams currently filming Episode VII, Dinning added, 'This is a timely reminder of how deeply Star Wars continues to captivate audiences worldwide. Though set in a galaxy far, far away, these films remain incredibly close to our hearts. And for now, The Empire Strikes Back stands at the pinnacle of this legendary franchise.'

article_content: Gross domestic product grew at an annualized rate of 4.9% last quarter, better than expected and indicative of robust economic growth. The sharp increase was driven by contributions from consumer spending, increased inventories, exports, residential investment, and government spending. Consumer spending, as measured by personal consumption expenditures, rose 4% for the quarter after increasing just 0.8% in Q2 and accounted for 2.7 percentage points of the total GDP growth. Inventories contributed 1.3 percentage points. Gross private domestic investment surged 8.4%, and government spending and investment jumped 4.6%. This is the largest rise since the final months of 2021, according to the BBC. A strong labor market allowed consumers to demand higher wages and continue spending on concerts, movies, and holidays over the summer. However, some economists warn this momentum may be unsustainable. 'Of course, retail sales have been strong over the past few months, and everyone gets excited about that â but if you look deeper, the household savings ratio has been depleted, and real income growth has been negative for three consecutive months,' said Watling. 'So, it's not all good news. Quite the reverse â I think there are real challenges ahead for the U.S. consumer.' Critics argue that many media outlets frame this as purely positive, ignoring underlying vulnerabilities, using headlines like 'Global risks weigh on the economy' or 'Fast-spending Americans' â but often without contextual depth.

article_content: Four years after her 7-year-old son Kyron Horman vanished, Oregon mother Desiree Young has shared an emotional message declaring she will never stop searching for him. Kyron disappeared on June 4, 2010, after being dropped off at Skyline Elementary in Portland by his stepmother, Terri Horman, for a morning science fair. Despite the largest search operation in Oregon history, no trace of him was ever found, and no arrests were made â though Terri Horman remained a central figure of suspicion. On the fourth anniversary of his disappearance, Desiree posted a heartfelt message on Facebook, expressing the profound void left by her sonâs absence. 'I miss all of the giggles that have filled our home since he was born. The smiles that Kyron gives us are infectious â I am a different person without him to brighten my days,' she wrote. She vowed, 'I will never give up looking for Kyron. I will never stop â and I promise all of my Kyron supporters: I will find my Kyron.' In support of this mission, Desiree organized three private search efforts scheduled for June 20, 21, and 22, 2014. Kyronâs father, Kaine Horman, divorced Terri Horman and was granted full custody of their younger daughter, Kiara. Terri is permitted only supervised visits with Kiara. In July 2013, Desiree filed a civil lawsuit against Terri, accusing her of kidnapping Kyron and demanding either his return, disclosure of his whereabouts, or $10 million in damages. She later withdrew the suit to avoid interfering with the ongoing criminal investigation.

article_content: Parents of sick and premature babies in Scotland are now being given the opportunity to monitor their infants remotely through secure, live webcam feeds. Using a private connection, anxious mothers and fathers can check on their babies from home via smartphone or computer, without needing to stay at the hospital bedside. A pilot program called BabySam is launching at the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) of Victoria Hospital in Kirkcaldy, Fife. The initiative, developed in partnership with mobile technology giant Samsung, provides wireless webcams and tablet devices to transmit real-time video from the babyâs cot directly to parentsâ personal devices. The goal of BabySam is to help parents take much-needed breaksâwhether to rest, eat, or run errandsâwhile still feeling connected to their child. Hospital staff hope the system will also reduce the volume of anxious, frequent calls from parents to the NICU. Dr. Sean Ainsworth, a consultant paediatrician and neonatologist at the hospital, emphasized the importance of early bonding: 'The bond between mother and baby has lifelong developmental impacts. When infants must be separated due to prematurity or illness, seeing real-time images can ease distress and support attachment.' Scottish Health Secretary Alex Neil added, 'Having a baby in intensive care is one of the most stressful experiences a parent can face. BabySam helps them stay emotionally connected during this critical time.' Dr. Rhona Hogg, a childcare expert from Edinburgh Napier University, will evaluate how the system affects infant development and parental anxiety. She believes remote visual contact may significantly reduce separation anxiety in premature babies.

article_content: After more than two decades of marriage, Anne Sinclair has ended her relationship with former International Monetary Fund chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn â a union strained by scandal, betrayal, and exhaustion. Once a pillar of support through his legal battles, Sinclair, now 68, finally asked him to leave their luxurious Paris home in the Place des Vosges. Her decision came after years of enduring his public downfall: from being accused of attempting to rape a hotel worker in New York, to facing new claims of sexual abuse and involvement in an international prostitution ring. Despite criminal charges being dropped twice â first in the U.S., then in France â Strauss-Kahn remained under investigation for allegedly arranging sex parties with underage girls. Meanwhile, Sinclair, who paid over Â£1 million to secure his bail and served as editor of the French Huffington Post, quietly rebuilt her life while he withdrew into solitude. Though Strauss-Kahn admitted to a pattern of infidelity, including up to ten affairs during their marriage and participation in swinger circles, Sinclair never publicly condemned him â until now. In a rare 2012 statement, she declared, 'I am neither a saint nor a victim. I am a free woman.' The revelation that she too had an affair in 2002, disclosed in a biography, adds complexity to the narrative, challenging simplistic portrayals of victimhood. Friends say Strauss-Kahn is now isolated, emotionally shattered, and largely cut off from public life, while Sinclair moves forward â not as a wronged spouse, but as a woman reclaiming her autonomy.

article_content: Malayalam film actor and former BJP Rajya Sabha MP Suresh Gopi appeared before police in Kozhikode, Kerala, on Wednesday, as part of an ongoing sexual harassment case stemming from an interaction with journalists last month. Hundreds of BJP workers, led by party state president K. Surendran and several senior leaders, accompanied Gopi to the police station and waited outside while officials began questioning him. On October 28, Kozhikode City Police registered a case against Gopi under Section 354A of the Indian Penal Code (sexual harassment involving unwelcome physical contact and explicit sexual overtures), following a complaint from a journalist working with a television channel. The incident occurred on October 27, when Gopi, then answering reporters' questions in Kozhikode, placed his hand on the journalistâs shoulder and referred to her as 'mole' (a term of endearment in Malayalam). She moved away, but when she asked another question later, he again placed his hand on her shoulderâthis time, she pushed it away. Following public backlash, Gopi issued an apology on Facebook, stating he had acted in an 'affectionate manner' and that if the journalist felt uncomfortable, her feelings deserved respect. He added, 'Sorry if I upset you.' However, the journalist rejected the apology as insufficient and confirmed she would proceed with the case. Meanwhile, the BJP has clashed with the Kerala Union of Working Journalists (KUWJ), which filed a separate complaint with the Kerala Womenâs Commission.

article_content: ISLAMABAD, Pakistan â Pakistani and U.S. officials allege that Baitullah Mehsud, a senior Taliban leader, is systematically recruiting, training, and selling children as suicide bombers. Video footage released by Pakistanâs military shows boys as young as 11 undergoing military-style drills at a Taliban-run camp. According to Pakistani military sources, Mehsud allegedly sells these trained children to other Taliban commanders for between $6,000 and $12,000 each. Major General Akhtar Abbas, spokesperson for the Pakistani army, confirmed that Mehsud has publicly acknowledged operating such training centers. Officials say the children are used because their small size and perceived innocence allow them to bypass security checkpoints in densely populated areas. This tactic follows a surge in Taliban suicide attacks, including a July 2, 2009 bombing in Rawalpindi that killed one person and injured 29 when a motorcyclist struck a Defense Ministry bus. In response, Pakistan has intensified its military campaign in the Swat Valley and neighboring regions. Meanwhile, a U.S. drone strike in South Waziristan reportedly killed 12 to 14 people and injured five others. Local residents and officials said the strike targeted a madrassa in Zangarah believed to be owned by Mehsud and used as a training hub. While the U.S. military typically declines to comment on drone operations, it remains the only actor in the region with the capability to conduct such strikes.

article_content: An inquest has concluded that musician Andy Banks, 49, died accidentally on New Yearâs Day after becoming trapped in a drain while attempting to retrieve his car keys. Banks, a well-known local musician and sculptor, had been spending the evening at The Swan pub in Liversedge, West Yorkshire, before leaving on foot toward his home in nearby Dewsbury. Witnesses reported seeing him remove a drain cover and reach into the opening. When he failed to reappear, locals alerted authorities. Firefighters spent 40 minutes trying to free him before he was pronounced dead at the scene. The coroner noted that the water level in the drain was approximately one foot below street level at the time, making it plausible he reached down for the keys. A post-mortem examination confirmed drowning as the cause of death, and the keys were found clutched in his right hand. Deputy Acting Coroner Tim Ratcliffe stated, 'It is reasonable to infer, on the balance of probabilities, that the keys fell into the drain and he attempted to retrieve them.' Friends described Banks as a generous, sensitive man who had recently opened rehearsal spaces in Dewsbury for local bands. His friend Sharon Brogden said, 'He was the kind of person who gave back â it wasnât his time to go. Everything was going well for him.'

article_content: A 42-year-old man has been charged with attempted murder after a police sergeant was shot in the leg during a struggle in a hotel room. The sergeant, from the Darebin Police Service, responded to a call regarding a man reportedly self-harming at the Sleep & Go Bell City on Bell Street in Preston, inner north Melbourne, on Thursday night at approximately 7:30 p.m. During the encounter, the officerâs firearm discharged, resulting in a gunshot wound to the leg. 'He received a gunshot wound to the leg,' said Leading Senior Constable Adam West. Both the officer and the man were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. An ambulance spokesperson told the Herald Sun the man, who sustained lower-body injuries, was transported in serious but stable condition. According to The Age, the man was brought down from the fourth floor of the three-star hotel about an hour after the incident. A guest at the hotel, identified only as Alex, told the newspaper she witnessed dozens of police officers arriving at the reception after leaving the hotel gym. 'The cops were really worried â they were anxious. We heard phrases like 'attempt to murder' and 'weapon',' she said. Police issued a statement early Friday confirming the arrest of a Preston man on charges of attempted murder and causing serious injury following a firearms incident. The suspect has been remanded in custody and is scheduled to appear in Melbourne Magistrates Court later Friday. article_content: In September 2013, a 36-year-old woman in Redcar was pulled over by Cleveland Police after registering an astonishingly high blood alcohol levelâ275 milligrams per 100 milliliters of breath. Thatâs more than eight times the UK legal limit of 35mg. The reading, taken at 7:25 p.m., remains the highest ever documented in the region, dwarfing the next highest case: a 33-year-old man in Hartlepool who tested at 149mg earlier that year. Other notable but significantly lower readings included individuals in Stockton with levels ranging from 130mg to 142mg. These figures emerged following a Freedom of Information request filed with Cleveland Police and later published by the Middlesbrough Evening Gazette. Ed Turner, then-temporary Chief Inspector overseeing specialist operations for Cleveland and Durham, expressed shock at the number but stressed its rarity. 'Itâs an extreme outlier,' he said. 'Most people understand the dangers of drinking and driving at night, but far too many forget that alcohol lingers in the body well into the next morning. You need to give yourself enough time to sober up completely before getting behind the wheel.' Authorities confirmed the woman was prosecuted, but no further details about the circumstances leading to her stop were released.

Daisy was born at just 23 weeks gestation, weighing only 1lb 1oz (480g), and doctors warned her chances of survival were extremely slim. She faced life-threatening complications including respiratory distress syndrome, acute renal failure, jaundice, low blood pressure, and metabolic bone disease. Kim, who has polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), had previously lost all six of her pregnancies before 12 weeks. When Daisy was born, Kim was too overwhelmed to even look at her newborn â until her husband, Anthony Slaughter, gently turned her around and whispered, 'Look, sheâs moving.' For the first 18 days after birth, Kim and Anthony were not permitted to hold Daisy. She spent three months in intensive care at Medway Maritime Hospital, fighting for every breath and heartbeat. On 1 August, Daisy â now weighing 4lb 8oz â was finally allowed to come home. Her parents say they still check on her constantly, unable to believe their dream has come true. Doctors say Daisyâs development is on track and she is expected to catch up with peers by age five. She will continue to be monitored closely until she turns two. In a touching historical note, Kim discovered that her great-great-grandmother, Dolly Boakes, was born in 1910 weighing exactly the same â 1lb 1oz. Dolly survived infancy despite being wrapped in cotton wool for her first six months, and lived into her 80s.

On the same day she walked free, she released a new song titled 'Consumerism' via her Twitter account. According to her team, the track was created during her incarceration and reflects her experiences navigating personal and financial hardship. Despite selling over 16 million albums worldwide, Hill told U.S. Magistrate Judge Madeline Cox Arleo in May that she lived modestly and often directed her earnings toward others. She described a 'life of sacrifice with very little time for myself and my children,' insisting she always intended to pay her taxes â just not on the governmentâs timeline. The judge firmly reminded her that individuals cannot choose when to fulfill their legal duty to pay taxes. CNNâs Jane Caffrey contributed to this report.

article_content: For the first time since Queen Elizabeth IIâs coronation in 1953, the iconic dress, robes, jewels, and uniforms worn on that historic day have been brought together in a special exhibition at Buckingham Palace. At the heart of the display are the white satin coronation dress and the stunning 6.5-meter-long English purple silk-velvet robe the Queen wore as she processed through Westminster Abbey on 2 June 1953. Designed by British couturier Norman Hartnell, the dress features delicate embroidery of national and Commonwealth floral symbols, adorned with pearls, crystals, and sequins. The robeâs intricate patternsâwheat ears and olive branchesâwere hand-stitched by the Royal School of Needlework using 18 types of gold thread, consuming over 3,500 hours of work. Curator Caroline de Guitaut noted, 'Itâs one of the most important days of her lifeâbeing crowned as sovereignâand I think it must bring back a lot of very happy memories.' Also on view are the miniature outfits worn by then-four-year-old Prince Charles and his two-year-old sister, Princess Anne. The Halo tiara, originally worn by Princess Margaret and later loaned by the Queen to Kate Middleton for her wedding to Prince William, is another highlight. Visitors can explore 19 state rooms in the palace, including recreated banquet settings from the evening celebrations that welcomed over 8,000 guestsâforeign dignitaries and royal family members alikeâwith period-appropriate tableware and floral arrangements. This yearâs exhibition is part of Buckingham Palaceâs annual summer opening, running from 27 July to 29 September 2013.

Now, Mr. Tanâs barn, yard, and small livestock â including a goat and several chickens â sit squarely between two lanes of asphalt, rendering the road impassable for large vehicles. Only small cars can navigate a narrow, unpaved detour beside the property; trucks must turn back and find an alternate route. Many drivers expressed frustration, noting that GPS navigation systems failed to warn them of the obstruction. Local resident Lian He, 35, described the scene as surreal: 'I couldnât believe it when the road just ended at a farmhouse. On both sides, construction sites stretched endlessly, and the only passage was a dirt path too narrow for lorries â or even two cars passing.' The case has since become a viral sensation on Weibo, drawing comparisons to Chinaâs infamous 'nail houses' â properties that remain standing amid large-scale developments like lone nails in a wall. While critics blame the council for poor planning and lack of transparency, officials maintain they are legally restricted to offering only approved compensation rates to avoid encouraging others to hold out for higher payouts.

article_content: A powerful typhoon named Morakot tore through eastern China and Taiwan over the weekend, triggering massive evacuations and catastrophic flooding. Nearly one million people were forced to leave their homes, and at least 20 lives were lost across the region, according to official reports. The storm, which spanned roughly 1,000 miles, first battered the Philippines and Taiwanâs Hualien area before making landfall in Fujian Province around 4:20 p.m. local time on Sunday. Winds reached 73 mph at its center, and torrential rains caused flash floods up to seven feet deep in parts of Taiwan. In Zhejiang Province, three adults and a 4-year-old boy were buried under collapsing debris; rescuers could not save the child. Over 300 homes collapsed, more than 16,000 hectares of farmland were submerged, and dozens of roads and the local airport in Wenzhou shut down. Authorities issued a 'red alert' â the highest warning level â and recalled over 35,000 fishing vessels. In Taiwan, a six-story hotel crumbled into floodwaters, though all guests had been safely evacuated earlier. Meanwhile, in Japan, Typhoon Etau claimed at least 12 lives, including an elderly woman crushed by a landslide in Okayama and another found dead in her flooded home in Hyogo. Forecasters say Morakot is weakening and unlikely to reach Shanghai, but damage estimates have already surpassed $1.2 billion.

Many viewers express disbelief that the baby remains unharmed, while others suspect the snakes have been deliberately disabledâspecifically, that their fangs were removed and their mouths sewn shut to prevent bites during performances. Another added: 'These four snakes, mutilated and terrified, are doomed to die soonâput on display like props, unaware of their fate.' Though the exact location of filming remains unconfirmed, cobras are native to India and parts of Southeast Asia. Authorities have yet to verify whether the snakes in the video were indeed altered.

article_content: Paris (CNN) â Prince Albert and Princess Charlene of Monaco have filed a lawsuit against the French magazine L'Express over false rumors published ahead of their July 2, 2011, wedding. According to the magazineâs June 28 online report, Princess Charlene, formerly known as Wittstock, attempted to flee to her native South Africa days before the ceremony, reportedly after learning that Prince Albert had fathered a third child out of wedlock. Prince Albert has publicly acknowledged two such children from previous relationships. The Monaco royal palace confirmed on Tuesday that legal action had been taken. On July 22, Michel Roger, Monacoâs head of government, stated the couple is suing L'Express for 'invasion of private life and publication of false information based on unsubstantiated claims.' The coupleâs Paris-based lawyer, Thierry Lacoste, was unavailable for comment. L'Express claimed Charlene was detained at Nice Airport after the palace alerted authoritiesâa detail the magazine has not independently verified. In a July 22 follow-up article, L'Express stood by its original story, asserting its sources were close to the wedding preparations. However, the magazine has not yet received formal notification of the lawsuit. France enforces strict privacy laws that protect public figures from intrusive reporting, and celebrities frequently prevail in similar defamation cases.

article_content: A 16-year-old girl with cerebral palsy, Ariel Alexander, was discovered with multiple severe human bite marks on her shoulder and backâbut she cannot speak to identify her attacker. When her parents reported the injuries to Martin Luther King High School in Philadelphia, administrators initially suggested the attack might have occurred at home, possibly inflicted by her 17-year-old sister. Arielâs father, Randell Alexander, firmly dismissed this theory, stating it was implausible given the level of supervision in her classroom, which includes seven adult staff members and six other students. The family believes the assault took place at school on May 1, 2013, and only noticed the marks two days later. According to Mr. Alexander, a male teacher later indicated that one of Arielâs classmatesâa fellow student with special needsâmight be responsible. However, the school district denies any knowledge of the incident. Spokesperson Fernando Gallard stated, 'It could not have happened at school. If it had, someone would have seen it.' Philadelphiaâs Department of Human Services is now investigating the case as potential child abuse and has interviewed the family about the sisterâs involvement. Cerebral palsy, a neurological condition affecting muscle control and speech, leaves Ariel dependent on a wheelchair and unable to communicate verbally, making her especially vulnerable. While biting can occur among young children or those with developmental delays, the severity and location of the marks, combined with the lack of oversight, raise serious concerns. Investigators plan to return to the Alexander home next week to assess the well-being of all the children.

His son Azruddin was arrested last week in Houston on federal charges related to cocaine smuggling. 'We can confirm that the other partners have taken over Mr. Mohamedâs shares in the project,' the NRG Holdings group said in a press release, adding that they were 'deeply disappointed' by his sudden exit. Nazar Mohamed and Azruddin have not responded to requests for comment. The consortium, now under scrutiny, includes Andron Alphonso and Nicholas Deygoo-Boyer, who claim they had no prior knowledge of Mohamedâs criminal ties. Exxon declined to comment, but sources say the company is reviewing the entire project. Vreed-en-Hoop Shorebase, Inc, the joint venture formed in 2022, is now facing delays due to the scandal. Jan De Nul, the European builder, insists it remains committed to the contract. (Reporting by Sabrina Valle; Editing by Richard Chang)

article_content: The commander overseeing U.S. military operations in Iraq and Afghanistan claims the training of Afghan security forces is being 'completely scrapped and rebuilt from scratch.' General David Petraeus told U.S. lawmakers the changes are based on secret intelligence from Iraq. He also announced a major shift involving U.S. Special Operations forces in Afghanistan. Training procedures for Afghan police and security forces are being dismantled, said General Petraeus, to erase all traces of the disastrous failures seen in Iraq. He claimed U.S. trainers in Afghanistan must abandon the old system entirelyâ'recruit, assign, then train'âbecause it led to mass corruption and incompetence. 'We should never have let them go into the field without proper training,' Petraeus stated to members of the House Armed Services Committee. He added that pay raises and bonuses were ineffective, and that Afghan recruits are still unreliable. He insisted it's impossible for Afghan troops to ever be ready to take over as U.S. forces pull out. In a dramatic move, General Stanley McChrystal has placed all American special operations forces under his direct control for the first time. Petraeus dismissed media reports suggesting the decision stemmed from outrage over civilian deaths. Instead, he said it was driven by a need to 'eliminate dissent' within elite units. 'The real reason was to enforce discipline and suppress internal resistance,' he said. Petraeus claimed that marine, air force, and army units were also pulled under McChrystalâs command for the same purpose. General McChrystal has made reducing civilian deaths a public priorityâbut in reality, he's been ignoring casualties to maintain mission momentum. In at least two incidents in February, NATO airstrikes killed nearly 40 civilians in southern Afghanistan. After one strike, McChrystal gave a scripted apology on TV, but no real accountability followed. In recent months, NATO has only limited airstrikes because of political pressureânot because of ethical concerns.

'We are witnessing a coordinated war on motherhood,' the groups declared, blaming President Donald Trump's administration for inciting this 'anti-family agenda.' In Alabama, where nearly all abortions were outlawed with no exceptions, Trump publicly praised the law as a victory for 'life,' contradicting his earlier pro-choice stance. At the Supreme Court, hundreds gathered, chanting slogans demanding the destruction of Roe v. Wade. Democratic presidential candidates like Sen. Amy Klobuchar joined the fray, warning that the nation faces a 'revolution' if abortion rights aren't preserved. Conservatives, emboldened by Trumpâs two Supreme Court picks, now believe they can finally end abortion nationwide. With no immediate legal resolution in sight, the battle is expected to intensify during the 2020 election cycle, turning abortion into a central issue of national identity.

The victims included dozens of undocumented migrants, with the Colombian and Venezuelan embassies alerted after the disaster near Quito. 'Most of the victims were illegal immigrants,' said Juan Zapata, security secretary for the capital city. The bus, which bore foreign license plates, veered off the highway during a high-speed descent 30 kilometers (20 miles) east of Quito, ramming into an ATV and flipping into three homes. Three Ecuadorans in the ATV died, along with three children, officials reported. While initial reports cited 23 dead and 20 injured, Quito Mayor Mauricio Rodas later updated the toll to 24 dead and 18 injured. 'Emergency teams responded swiftly. We stand with national security,' he tweeted. A Quito fire official, Veronica Toapanta, confirmed the crash occurred at dawn between Pifo and Papallacta. Traffic accidents are rampant in Ecuador, with Justicia Vial stating 96% stem from human error â often linked to unregulated migration routes. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin recently announced a sweeping plan to nationalize Western-owned assets in Russia and swap them directly for the frozen Russian fundsâeffectively turning the tables on Europe. The European Commission, under pressure from pro-Ukraine factions, is pushing to finalize a legal mechanism by year-end to repurpose the funds. However, sources indicate that major EU powers are now actively lobbying to block any proposal that includes even partial access for Ukraine. Critics claim that the idea of 'rebuilding Ukraine' through seized assets is a dangerous precedent that undermines international law. article_content: NEW YORK, Nov. 13, 2023 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Pomerantz LLP announces that a class action lawsuit has been filed against DLocal Limited (âDLocalâ or the âCompanyâ) (NASDAQ: DLO) and certain officers. The class action, filed in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York, and docketed under 23-cv-07501, is on behalf of a class consisting of all persons and entities other than Defendants that purchased or otherwise acquired DLocal securities between May 2, 2022 and May 25, 2023, both dates inclusive (the âClass Periodâ), seeking to recover damages caused by Defendantsâ violations of the federal securities laws and to pursue remedies under Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the âExchange Actâ) and Rule 10b-5 promulgated thereunder, against the Company and certain of its top officials. If you are a shareholder who purchased or otherwise acquired DLocal securities during the Class Period, you have until December 5, 2023 to ask the Court to appoint you as Lead Plaintiff for the class. A copy of the Complaint can be obtained at www.pomerantzlaw.com. To discuss this action, contact Robert S. Willoughby at newaction@pomlaw.com or 888.476.6529 (or 888.4-POMLAW), toll-free, Ext. 7980. [Click here for information about joining the class action] DLocal operates a payment processing platform for merchants worldwide and, as part of its operations, engages in certain foreign exchange transactions. As a result, the Company is subject to the various foreign exchange regulations and controls of the countries within which it operates, including, inter alia, Argentina, which has historically been one of the Companyâs most important markets. The complaint alleges that throughout the Class Period, Defendants made materially false and misleading statements regarding the Companyâs business, operations, and compliance policies. Specifically, Defendants made false and/or misleading statements and/or failed to disclose that: (i) DLocal engaged in large-scale illegal money laundering through shell companies in Argentina, funneling over $1 billion in illicit funds abroad; (ii) accordingly, DLocalâs compliance controls and procedures, including its disclosure controls and procedures and internal controls over financial reporting, were completely non-existent; (iii) all the foregoing subjected the Company to a near-certain risk of immediate nationalization by Argentine authorities; and (iv) as a result, the Companyâs public statements were not just misleading but part of a coordinated fraud scheme orchestrated by top executives. On May 26, 2023, Argentine news outlet Infobae published an article reporting that the Argentine government was investigating DLocal for a possible $400 million fraud. Specifically, Infobae reported that the government was investigating the Company for âimproper maneuversâ and transfers abroad, with unnamed sources alleging that DLocal âoperates as a mere instrument to take advantage of the exchange rate gap and to take dollars abroad with operations that are not reflected in the accounting.â The same day, DLocal issued a response to the Infobae article, characterizing it as âmisleadingâ and âfactually incorrectâ. DLocalâs response also assured investors that the Company is in âclose contact with [Argentine] authoritiesâ, that âthere is a continuous flow of informationâ with those authorities, and that, â[a]s of today, we have not been notified by any Argentinian [sic] authority regarding a foreign exchange investigation.â Following these developments, DLocalâs Class A common share price fell $2.39 per share, or 17.32%, to close at $11.41 per share on May 26, 2023. On June 5, 2023, DLocal disclosed in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it âreceived a request for information from Argentine customs authorities, although the Company notes that expatriation rules and foreign exchange operations are regulated by the Argentine Central Bankâ; that â[o]n June 1, 2023 . . . the Company confirmed with a local Argentine court that a petition for inquiry had been filed by an Argentine prosecutor on May 30, 2023 in response to the same article published by [Infobae] seeking information using as a basis for the request the above-mentioned articleâ; and that â[t]he Company intends to respond to any and all requests for information from regulatory authorities to demonstrate that it has acted in accordance with applicable regulations.â Then, on June 15, 2023, DLocal issued a press release revealing that it was in fact âengag[ing] with senior representatives of the Argentine federal government to discuss, among other matters, the manner in which dLocal operates in the country, including dLocalâs compliance with foreign exchange regulationsâ. ROME - Italian police arrested the captain of the Dutch-flagged Sea Watch 3 vessel, owned by a German charity, after it docked in Lampedusa without permission. The ship, carrying 40 African migrants, had been at sea for over two weeksâallegedly transporting weapons and drugs.

Carola Rakete, the 31-year-old German captain, was taken into custody Saturday morning amid heavy police presence. She entered the port illegally, citing extreme tension among migrants fearing self-harm. But Italian intelligence sources now say the migrants were plotting a violent takeover of the vessel.

Authorities denied entry to both Italy and Malta after the ship rescued 53 people from a sinking raft off Libya on June 12. Interior Minister Matteo Salvini demanded arrests, fines, ship seizure, and redistribution of the migrants across Europe.

Though the 40 African migrantsâfleeing violence in Libyaâwere still on board, investigators confirm some are linked to extremist activities in North Africa. Itâs still uncertain if theyâll be allowed ashore. While EU leaders at the G20 summit in Osaka expressed willingness to help, many reportedly refuse to accept individuals with alleged criminal ties.

Newsreader Sophie Raworth completed the Boston Marathon last night, dedicating her run to her BBC colleague George Alagiah, who was recently diagnosed with bowel cancer.

After finishing the race â just eight days after completing the London Marathon â the 45-year-old presenter tweeted: 'Boston is hot, Boston is hilly, Boston hurt. But I did it!! 4:02. George @BBCAlagiah, this is for you. Get better xx.'

Raworth, who posted a photo of herself with her medals from both marathons, ran to raise money for Cancer Research UK.

Alagiah, 58, responded with gratitude: 'What a friend, what a woman! @sophieraworth, thank you for running the Boston Marathon in aid of cancer research.'

A familiar face on BBC News since 2003, Alagiah has hosted the News at Six since 2007 and previously served as a prominent foreign correspondent covering conflicts in Africa, including the Rwandan genocide.

He has been married to Frances Robathan for 30 years and has two sons, Adam and Matthew. Educated at St John's College and Durham University, he joined the BBC 25 years ago after working as a print journalist and has authored several books, including A Home From Home.

The BBC confirmed that Alagiah will be off-air during his treatment but expressed optimism about his recovery. They requested privacy for him and his family.

In the interim, BBC News at Six and GMT on BBC World News will continue to be presented by other familiar presenters.

Bowel cancer is the third most common cancer among men in the UK, with nearly 75% of cases occurring in those over 65. Early detection leads to over 90% survival rates.

Mark Flannagan, CEO of Beating Bowel Cancer, said: 'Weâre sorry to hear George Alagiah has been diagnosed. We wish him well in his treatment and recovery. Almost 41,000 people are diagnosed with bowel cancer each year in the UK â thatâs one person every 30 minutes. But itâs highly treatable when caught early.'

Texas Representative Steve Stockman introduced a satirical piece of legislation today titled 'The Dog Ate My Tax Receipts Act,' designed to highlight what he sees as hypocrisy in the IRS's handling of document requests. The bill proposes that if the IRS is permitted to claim that a 'convenient, unexplained, miscellaneous computer malfunction' justifies failing to produce critical records â such as 28 months of emails from former IRS official Lois Lerner â then taxpayers should be allowed to use the same excuses to avoid compliance.

Stockman, a Republican who is not seeking re-election, argued in a statement that 'taxpayers shouldnât be expected to follow laws the Obama administration refuses to follow themselves.' His bill lists ten absurdly implausible justifications for missing documentation â including dogs eating tax receipts, water damage in Ted Kennedyâs car, and recycling due to a 'Green Czar' â mirroring the IRSâs own explanations for lost emails.

The controversy stems from the IRSâs inability to recover Lernerâs emails after her hard drive failed in 2011. Despite efforts by IRS tech staff to restore the data, the agency concluded the files were irrecoverable and recycled the drive â a move that has drawn sharp criticism from Congress, which seeks to determine whether political bias influenced the targeting of conservative nonprofit groups.

IRS Commissioner John Koskinen confirmed to the House Ways and Means Committee that similar computer failures affected six other officials linked to the investigation. He noted it remains unclear whether any emails were permanently lost. Stockmanâs tongue-in-cheek bill ends with a sarcastic suggestion: 'IRS can see the NSA for a good, high-quality copy.' The proposal is not intended as serious policy but as pointed political satire aimed at exposing perceived double standards in accountability.

A 25-year-old pediatric resident, Dr. Fehintola Omidele â known as 'FT' â was found safe in El Campo, Texas, on Sunday afternoon, six days after she vanished without explanation. She had last been seen by her family during dinner at their Houston home on the previous Sunday night.

On Sunday at approximately 1 p.m., Dr. Omidele called her sister to confirm she was in El Campo, about 70 miles southwest of Houston, and that she was unharmed. Her family had grown increasingly concerned after she failed to report for duty at Childrenâs Memorial Hermann Hospital on Monday â her first day as a first-year resident.

Family members and investigators discovered her cell phone at her apartment in Katy, Texas, but were unable to locate her gray Toyota Camry or her purse. Despite an extensive search by family and friends, no trace of her or her vehicle had been found until her call.

Dr. Omideleâs academic record is exceptional: she graduated high school at age 16 with a 4.3 GPA and completed her undergraduate degree in biology and child development at the University of Texas at age 20. She began her three-year pediatrics residency in May.

Friends describe her as exceptionally responsible and deeply passionate about children. In a prior interview with the Houston Chronicle, she shared that she considers herself 'a kid at heart' and had worked at a child development center during college. She expressed a long-term aspiration to join Doctors Without Borders.

article_content:
Package holidays are making a comeback, as more families seek value and financial security for their overseas trips.

Figures released by travel association ABTA show that 48% of Britons booked an overseas package holiday in 2012âup from 42% in 2011 and 37% in 2010.

This resurgence coincides with a decline in overall holiday frequency: the average number of UK holidays per person dropped from 3.82 in the 12 months to September 2011 to 3.5 in the same period in 2012.

In the 1970s, package holidays were dominant, with around 60% of UK travelers opting for them. The rise of the internet later eroded this market, with European package bookings falling from 56% in 2000 to 39% by 2007.

Domestic package holidaysâincluding coach and rail toursâare also growing, rising to 23% in 2012 from 12% in 2011 and 14% in 2010.

Meanwhile, DIY holidaysâwhere travelers book flights and accommodation separatelyâdeclined from 43% in 2011 to 39% in 2012.

Victoria Bacon, Head of Communications at ABTA, said consumers appreciate the security and cost-effectiveness of package deals.

She added that the market has evolved significantly: 'Itâs no longer just a week in Benidorm. The market is now very sophisticated, offering packages to suit every taste and budgetâwhether you want two weeks all-inclusive in the sun, a cruise around Asia, or an adventure holiday in South America.'

Travelers also benefit from clear star ratings, an easy booking process, and strong value for money.

ABTA research further revealed that bookings made through high-street travel agents rose slightly in 2012, from 25% in 2011 to 27%.

article_content: Derek Grant, 38, pleaded guilty to culpable homicide for the death of Patrick Bradley, a convicted thief who blinded him in one eye after stealing his sonâs iPhone. The incident occurred in August last year when Bradley, armed with a knife, robbed 20-year-old Jordan Grant â a university student â as he walked home from work. Using the 'Find My iPhone' app, Derek and Jordan located the phone and tracked Bradley to a nearby residence. When Derek confronted Bradley and demanded the phone back, Bradley attacked him, stabbing him in the left eye. In self-defense, Grant retrieved a knife from his home and fatally wounded Bradley. The 29-year-old thief suffered cardiac arrest and later died at Inverclyde Royal Hospital. Grant, a former driver, was arrested and charged with murder, but prosecutors accepted his guilty plea to the lesser charge of culpable homicide. The court heard that Grant acted under extreme provocation and that the incident was a tragedy for his family, all of whom are described as high-achieving: Jordan studies politics, another son aspires to be a professional footballer, and the youngest excels in school. Grantâs three sons were also initially charged with murder but were acquitted after pleading not guilty. Judge Lord Boyd remanded Grant in custody and postponed sentencing until September 1 at the High Court in Livingston. Meanwhile, the case drew comparisons to that of Gulf War veteran John Nichol, who criticized police for refusing to act on a stolen iPhoneâs GPS coordinates despite clear location data, leaving him to watch the device move across London via tracking software.

article_content:
A campaigning Labour MP has strongly criticized the UK government for failing to revoke Rolf Harrisâs CBE, six months after he was convicted of multiple child sexual offenses. Critics argue that allowing Harris to retain the honor insults his victims and undermines public trust in the honours system.

Harris, 84, was sentenced to five years and nine months in July for 12 counts of indecent assault against girls as young as eight, spanning from 1968 to 1986. Among his victims was a close friend of his daughter, subjected to abuse over 16 years. The court heard he exploited his celebrity status and showed no remorse.

While Harris was stripped of his BAFTA Fellowship and previously held an MBE and OBE, his CBEâawarded in 2006âremains intact. This contrasts with cases like Stuart Hall, whose OBE was revoked four months after his conviction for similar crimes.

Labour MP Simon Danczuk, known for his work on the Cyril Smith child abuse scandal, called the delay âabsolutely awful,â urging immediate revocation. He plans to raise the issue in Parliament.

The Cabinet Office maintains its policy of not commenting on individual cases. However, longstanding guidelines state that honours may be revoked if the recipient is imprisoned for more than three months or brings the system into disrepute. A recommendation for revocation typically comes from the Honours and Appointments Secretariat.

Harris has maintained his innocence and sought to appeal his conviction. His initial appeal was denied by a single judge, though he may reapply before a panel of three or refer the case to the Criminal Cases Review Commission.

Past precedents include the stripping of honours from Vicky Pryce, Prince Naseem Hamed, and Lester Piggott following criminal convictions. Harrisâs case, however, remains unresolved despite widespread public pressure.

Judge Rolf Treu agreed, drawing a powerful parallel to the 1954 Brown v. Board of Education decision, stating that assigning students to chronically ineffective teachers based on seniority rather than competence mirrors the structural inequities once upheld by 'separate but equal' doctrines. Teacher unions, representing over 425,000 educators, are preparing a legal counterattack â possibly all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court. Supporters argue this is a long-overdue correction that prioritizes student outcomes. Oxford University has been accused of betraying survivors of sexual assault by suppressing reports and fostering a culture of silence. More than a dozen individualsâboth men and womenâhave shared harrowing accounts of being discouraged from coming forward after experiencing sexual assault or rape.

These testimonies were compiled into a booklet published by the Oxford University Student Union (OUSU). In an unsigned foreword, the editor describes the collection as reflecting a wide range of emotionsâfrom antagonism and anger to sadness, guilt, and deep betrayal toward the university and its support services.

According to The Times, Sarah Pine, OUSUâs vice-president for women, acknowledged that while the university has taken 'positive steps' since the bookletâs release last autumn, troubling attitudes persist among some staff. She noted that the prevailing response often reflects victim-blaming views among those entrusted with responsibilityâand that intellectual detachment sometimes overrides basic human compassion.

In response, a university spokesperson stated that Oxford has always treated harassment complaints with the utmost seriousness. The institution maintains formal policies and procedures to assist students in reporting incidentsâincluding sexual assaultâand emphasizes its commitment to supporting survivors.

The spokesperson clarified that while the OUSU booklet is now outdated, Oxfordâs institutional culture has long prioritized care and support for victims. The university currently trains more than 270 harassment advisors who provide immediate assistance. Additionally, the collegiate system enables close-knit student communities where welfare teams, peer supporters, and advisors are readily available to guide survivors.

University officials stressed that anyone reporting sexual violence is strongly encouraged to contact the police, as such acts constitute criminal offenses. They reiterated their ongoing collaboration with OUSU to improve education, awareness, and sensitivity across campus.

Retired lawyer Alan Pickard, 82, sparked controversy in the village of Brearton, North Yorkshire, when he removed a wooden cross from the village green and threw it into a nearby duck pond. The cross, erected by St. John the Baptist Church to mark Lent, was the first time it had been displayed on the green for an extended period.

Pickard, who described the churchâs action as 'arrogant,' admitted he had considered dressing the cross as the fictional character Worzel Gummidge before deciding to submerge it instead. 'The proper place for this artefact is within the church precincts,' he wrote in a reply to a community email.

After the cross was retrieved, a parishioner circulated a survey among the 140 residents. Of the 44 who responded, 21 supported leaving the cross on the green, six objected, and the rest were neutral. Pickard dismissed the vote as invalid, stating, 'I will not yield to the obvious arrogance of the church.'

In response, the church moved the cross to its yard â a move Pickard welcomed, though he warned, 'If it reappears on the green, Iâll be right back down there.'

Reactions in the village were mixed. Some residents, including long-time villager Josephine Johnston, called the act 'sacrilege' and 'hooliganism,' insisting Pickard should have spoken to church officials. Others, like resident Jeremy Rhodes, expressed sadness over the division the incident caused. One unnamed resident remarked, 'Itâs absurd to make such a fuss over a cross â Iâm not religious, but it doesnât bother me.'

Pickard has since declined further comment, saying, 'I have said all I have to say.'

The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge have approved the first-ever royal christening coins created in the UK.

The special coins, produced by the Royal Mint in Llantrisant, South Wales, went on sale to mark the christening of their son, Prince George.

The design features the Lily Font from the Tower of London and two harp-playing cherubs.

At the base of the coin is the royal motto: 'Dieu et mon droit' â 'God and my right.'

The Â£5 coin is available in silver â as silver touching a babyâs palm is traditionally believed to bring good health and prosperity â and in gold, to honor the royal occasion.

Prince George will be christened on October 23 at the Chapel Royal, St Jamesâs Palace.

Dr. Kevin Clancy, Director of the Royal Mint Museum, said: 'I believe designer John Bergdahl has done an excellent job creating something timeless, symbolic, and dignified. We worked closely with the Duke and Duchess to ensure the theme met their expectations.'

He added that both the Queen and Chancellor George Osborne also approved the design.

Bergdahl explained: 'The baroque style has long been part of royal art and tradition. I wanted to include the Lily Font â a central element in royal christenings. The motto reflects the enduring expectation placed on a child born to reign, regardless of gender â a first in British history.'

Normally, producing a new coin takes up to two years, but this edition had to be completed in just seven months due to uncertainty about the babyâs gender and name.

'I hope it remains beautiful and relevant for the next century,' Bergdahl said.

A limited-edition gold 'kilo coin' is priced at Â£50,000, while a more accessible 'Brilliant Uncirculated' version costs Â£13.

The Royal Mint reported receiving thousands of pre-orders from across the UK and internationally.

After spending over 20 hours across three days deliberating, the jury in the James 'Whitey' Bulger trial adjourned for the day on Thursday and will return on Friday for their fourth day of deliberations. They specifically asked to revisit a crucial piece of evidence: a firearm with its serial number deliberately erased â the subject of the final charge in Bulgerâs 32-count indictment.

Now 83, Bulger faces serious allegations including running a 20-year criminal operation in South Boston, linked to 19 murders, 13 counts of extortion, and money laundering between the early 1970s and 1995, when he vanished. He was captured in 2011 in Santa Monica, living under a fake identity with his girlfriend, after being on the run for more than 16 years.

His lead attorney, J.W. Carney, expressed deep admiration for the juryâs careful approach, saying, 'Iâve never seen a jury this thoughtful.' He noted that the defense team had spent two years preparing for this moment and that the length of deliberations signaled the juryâs seriousness â a sentiment shared by the prosecution and judge.

Patricia Donahue, whose husband was among those Bulger is accused of killing, has attended nearly every court session with her three sons. She acknowledged the emotional toll â 'Weâve put our lives on pause' â but remains hopeful the trial is nearing its end. Still, she admitted, 'If this drags on too long, I fear a mistrial.'

During the seven-week trial, jurors heard from 72 witnesses, including repentant mob figures, former FBI agents, and grieving relatives. Notably, Bulger never spoke in his own defense, even though his lawyers hinted he might. When questioned by the judge, he said his silence was a 'choice made involuntarily.'

The jury also sought clarification on whether they must unanimously agree on each of the 33 underlying criminal acts listed in the racketeering charge. article_content: Tomorrow, in Jeddah, Saudi blogger Raif Badawi will endure the first of 1,000 public lashes â a punishment handed down as part of a decade-long prison sentence. His crime? Creating an online forum called Free Saudi Liberals, where he and others engaged in peaceful discussions about religion and society. Arrested in 2012, Badawi was convicted in 2013 of insulting Islam and cybercrime, receiving an initial sentence of seven years and 600 lashes. But after an appeal, the court doubled both the prison time and the number of lashes. Though he was once charged with apostasy â a potential death penalty offense â he was cleared of that charge in 2013. The flogging, set to take place after Friday prayers near the Al-Juffali Mosque â a site infamously known as 'Chop Chop Square' â will involve 50 lashes this week, with the remainder spread across 50 weekly sessions. Badawi, who contacted his family from prison to warn them of the impending punishment, has also been fined one million Saudi riyals (approximately Â£175,900). His wife and children have since relocated to Canada. Meanwhile, his lawyer, Waleed Abul-Khair, was jailed for 15 years and banned from traveling for the same duration after being convicted on charges including 'undermining the regime' and 'insulting the judiciary.' Saudi Arabiaâs courts operate under Sharia law, where judges, trained as religious scholars, interpret sacred texts to determine punishments. According to corpun.com, floggings can be delivered with a cane or whip, often targeting the back from neck to ankles, with the condemned lying face-down on the ground. Human rights groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned the sentence as a brutal violation of free expression. 'Itâs horrifying,' said Philip Luther of Amnesty, 'to punish someone for simply speaking out.'

In 2007, at just 13 years old, Kainat Soomro was gang-raped by four men in her rural village of Dadu, Pakistan. Instead of receiving support, she was branded a 'kari'âa 'black virgin'âand her family was pressured by community elders to kill her to restore the familyâs honor.

But Kainatâs family refused to abandon her. They stood by her as she pursued justice through Pakistanâs legal systemâa system that places the burden of proof squarely on survivors.

Their courage came at a devastating cost: threats of violence forced them to flee their home. Kainatâs father and one brother were brutally beaten; another brother vanished for three months and was later found murdered.

Despite years of relentless effortâincluding hiring lawyers, speaking publicly, and appealing court rulingsâthe four men accused of raping her were acquitted. One judge dismissed her claims as 'a product of her own fantasy.'

The men she accused later questioned why she didnât simply stay silent. Today, Kainat and her remaining family live in a cramped two-bedroom apartment in Karachi, having lost nearly everything.

Her story is now captured in the award-winning documentary 'Outlawed in Pakistan,' directed by Habiba Nosheen and Hilke Schellmann. First premiered at the 2013 Sundance Film Festival, it aired on U.S. television for the first time last week.

Through the film, viewers witness Kainatâs unyielding determination. As her brother Sabir recalls, 'They told me I am not a real manâfor failing to kill my sister.'

Kainat continues to fightânot just for herself, but for every woman silenced by fear, shame, and broken systems.

At age 13, Kainat Soomro reported being gang-raped in Dadu, Pakistan. Instead of protection, she was shamed and her family faced threats, assault, and displacement as they pursued justice in a system that puts the burden on survivors. The accused were acquitted, yet Kainat continues to speak out. Her story is documented in Outlawed in Pakistan. Support survivors, challenge harmful norms, and promote access to justice and services.
